metadata.title: Clustering Noisy Signals with Structured Sparsity Using Time-Frequency Representation

extraction_notes.note: theorem or definition: the sentence states the standard L^2 wavelet expansion and in its 'where' clause names the scaling and wavelet coefficients; kept as one external theorem, since splitting the sentence is not allowed.
theorem or remark: two qualitative cited facts (wavelets not translation invariant; fine coefficients unstable under deformations, Mallat 2012) stated as motivation for the scattering transform.
The 'three-step procedure' of wavelet shrinkage is written as one formula W^{-1} eta(W x), so no algorithm_step could be cut from it without splitting the display; AP4 has zero steps.

Table 1 (real-data ARI for seven methods) and Table 2 (scattering parameters) carry most of the empirical content; they are represented only by the claims that read them, including the Table 1 caption claim ClP15.
The scattering transform is built sentence by sentence (filters, layers, scale path, sampling, final layer); each symbol-introducing sentence is its own definition rather than one algorithm node.

Not extracted: the simulation set-up (test curves, packages, baselines), dataset descriptions, figure captions, the Wasserman GMM mention, and the future-work directions other than the theoretical-guarantees question.

metadata.extraction_comment: The SPARCScatter method reported in Table 1 is never defined in the text; it is presumably sparse K-means (ProbP1/AP5) on scattering coefficients, possibly followed by the feature-selection re-clustering AP8 (the 0.91 Growth figure matches ClP9).

nodes.name: SPARCWave
nodes.statement: We introduce SPARCWave \: -- Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- a framework of methods for sparse clustering of noisy signals, which \textbf{(i)} uses ``global" cross-signal information for smoothing and dimensionality reduction simultaneously, by sparse clustering using time-frequency representation, \textbf{(ii)} is geared towards preserving clustering information (rather than individual signals -- see Figure \ref{fig:sim}), \textbf{(iii)} exploits structure in the signal representation, such as multi-scale properties in univariate signals and interdependencies in multivariate signals, and \textbf{(iv)} uses the scattering transform \cite{anden2014deep,bruna2010classification,bruna2013invariant}, that generates features invariant to translations and dilations and robust to small deformations in both time and frequency. We use the natural structure in the scattering coefficients in our sparse clustering method.
nodes.genus: a framework of methods for sparse clustering of noisy signals
differentia: uses ``global" cross-signal information for smoothing and dimensionality reduction simultaneously
is geared towards preserving clustering information
exploits structure in the signal representation
nodes.statement_short: SPARCWave: sparse clustering of noisy signals in a time-frequency (wavelet / scattering) representation, exploiting structured sparsity.

nodes.name: Wavelet-denoise-then-cluster (Giacofci et al.)
nodes.statement: Giacofci et al. \cite{giacofci2013wavelet} first perform wavelets-based denoising for each signal, and then use model-based clustering on the union set of non-zero coefficients after shrinkage.
nodes.statement_short: Denoise each signal by wavelet shrinkage, then model-based clustering on the union of surviving coefficients.

nodes.name: Multi-scale energy features (Antoniadis et al.)
nodes.statement: Antoniadis et al. \cite{antoniadis2013clustering} use the fact that the overall energy of a signal $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^T$ can be decomposed into a multi-scale view of the energy, and propose extracting features that involve averaging wavelet coefficients in each scale and measuring each scale's relative importance.
nodes.statement_short: Cluster on features that average wavelet coefficients within each scale and weigh each scale's relative energy.

nodes.statement: extracting features that involve averaging wavelet coefficients in each scale
nodes.statement_short: Average wavelet coefficients per scale

nodes.name: Scale averaging loses time information
nodes.statement: However, this averaging loses the time information: two different signals with the same power spectrum will have very similar $\mathbf{v}_{(j)}$ coefficients, which may lead to clustering errors.
nodes.statement_short: Averaging all wavelets at a scale discards timing: signals with equal power spectra get similar features.

nodes.name: Dynamic Time Warping
nodes.statement: A common approach to dealing with deformations is the Dynamic Time Warping approach (DTW) \cite{berndt1994using}, which uses dynamic programming to align pairs of signals.
nodes.statement_short: DTW: align pairs of signals by dynamic programming before comparing them.

nodes.name: Wavelet family
nodes.statement: More formally, a wavelet family $\Psi_{j,k}$ is a set of functions generated by dilations and translations of a unique mother wavelet $\Psi$: \begin{equation} \Psi_{j,k}(t) = a^{\frac{j}{2}} \Psi(a^j t - k), \end{equation} where $j,k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $a>0$. The constant $a$ represents resolution in frequency, $j$ represents scale and $k$ translations.
differentia: generated by dilations and translations of a unique mother wavelet $\Psi$
nodes.statement_short: Wavelet family: dilations and translations $a^{j/2}\Psi(a^j t-k)$ of a mother wavelet $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Dilation-translation of the mother wavelet
nodes.statement: \Psi_{j,k}(t) = a^{\frac{j}{2}} \Psi(a^j t - k),
nodes.label: def:wave_funcs

nodes.name: Scaling function family
nodes.statement: We similarly define a family of functions $\phi_{0,k}$ derived from a scaling function $\phi(t)$ by using the dilation and translation formulation given in eq. (\ref{def:wave_funcs}).
differentia: derived from a scaling function $\phi(t)$ by using the dilation and translation formulation

nodes.name: Wavelet decomposition
nodes.statement: Any function $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ can then be decomposed in terms of these functions: \begin{equation} f(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k}\phi_{0,k}(t) + \sum_{j,k \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbf{v}_{j,k}\Psi_{j,k}(t) , \end{equation} where $c_{k} = \langle \phi_{0,k}(t),f(t) \rangle$ are the scaling coefficients, and $\mathbf{v}_{j,k} = \langle \Psi_{j,k}(t),f(t) \rangle$ are called the wavelet coefficients of $f(t)$.
conclusions: can then be decomposed in terms of these functions
nodes.statement_short: Every $L^2$ function expands in scaling functions and wavelets; the coefficients are inner products (scaling and wavelet coefficients).

nodes.name: Wavelet expansion of f
nodes.statement: f(t) = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} c_{k}\phi_{0,k}(t) + \sum_{j,k \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbf{v}_{j,k}\Psi_{j,k}(t) ,
nodes.label: eq:wavelet_basis

nodes.name: Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)
nodes.statement: This decomposition has a discrete version known as the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Given $x_1,\ldots, x_T$ forming a signal $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^T$ sampled at times $t=1,..,T$, where $T = 2^J$, and taking $a=2$, the DWT of $\mathbf{x}$ is given by taking $c_0$ and $v_{j,k}$ for $j=0,..,J-1$ and $k=0,..,2^j$ in eq. (\ref{eq:wavelet_basis}), where $\phi_{0,0}, \Psi_{j,k}$ are evaluated at $t=1,..,T$ to compute the (discrete) inner products $\langle \phi_{0,0}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$ and $\langle \Psi_{j,k}, \mathbf{x} \rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: DWT of a length-$T=2^J$ signal: the scaling coefficient $c_0$ and wavelet coefficients $v_{j,k}$ computed as discrete inner products.

nodes.name: DWT matrix form
nodes.statement: The DWT can be written conveniently in a matrix form $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}$ where $\mathbf{W}$ is an orthogonal matrix defined by the chosen $\Psi, \phi$, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the vector of coefficients $c_{0}, \Psi_{j,k}$ properly ordered.
nodes.statement_short: DWT as $\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$ with orthogonal $\mathbf{W}$ determined by $\Psi,\phi$.

nodes.name: Wavelet shrinkage denoising
nodes.statement: This property is typically used for signal denoising using a three-step procedure \cite{donoho1995noising}: \\ \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbf{x}} \equiv \mathbf{W}^{-1} \eta_{\lambda} (\mathbf{W} \mathbf{x}) \end{equation} where $\eta_{\lambda}$ is a nonlinear shrinkage (smoothing) operator, for example entry-wise soft-threshold operator with parameter $\lambda$: $\eta_{\lambda}(\mathbf{v}) = \text{sgn}(\mathbf{v})(|\mathbf{v}| - \lambda)_{+}$.
nodes.statement_short: Denoise by transforming to the wavelet domain, shrinking coefficients (e.g. soft-thresholding at $\lambda$), and inverting.

nodes.name: Wavelet shrinkage estimator
nodes.statement: \hat{\mathbf{x}} \equiv \mathbf{W}^{-1} \eta_{\lambda} (\mathbf{W} \mathbf{x})
nodes.label: eq:DWT_denoising

nodes.name: Signal instances and their DWT
nodes.statement: Consider $n$ instances (signal vectors) $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^T$, and let $\mathbf{v}^{(i)}$ be their DWT transforms.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals

nodes.name: Coordinate-wise squared distance
nodes.statement: Let $d_{i_{1},i_{2},j}$ be the squared (Euclidean) distance between $\mathbf{v}^{(i_1)}$ and $\mathbf{v}^{(i_2)}$ over coordinate $j$, $d_{i_{1},i_{2},j} \equiv (\mathbf{v}_j^{(i_1)}-\mathbf{v}_j^{(i_2)})^2$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals

nodes.name: Cluster index sets
nodes.statement: Let $C_{k}$ be the set of indices corresponding to cluster $k$ with $|C_k|=n_k$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals

nodes.name: Between Cluster Sum of Squares (BCSS)
nodes.statement: In standard K-means clustering, the goal is to maximize the \textit{Between Cluster Sum of Squares} (BCSS), which can be represented as a sum $1^T \mathcal{D}$ where $\mathcal{D}$ is a vector representing the contribution of the wavelet coefficient $j$ to the BCSS, with \begin{equation} \mathcal{D}_j \equiv \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i_{1},i_2=1}^{n} {d_{i_{1},i_{2},j } } - \sum_{k=1}^{K} { \frac{1}{n_{k}} \sum_{i_{1},i_{2} \in C_{k} }{ d_{i_{1},i_{2},j }}}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: K-means maximizes the BCSS $1^T\mathcal{D}$, where $\mathcal{D}_j$ is coordinate $j$'s between-cluster contribution.

nodes.name: Per-coordinate BCSS contribution
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.label: eq:BCSS

nodes.name: Feature weights and sparsity parameter
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^T$ be a vector of weights, and $s$ a tuning parameter bounding $\|\mathbf{w}\|_1$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals

nodes.name: Sparse K-means problem
nodes.statement: We get the following sparse K-means \cite{witten2010framework} constrained optimization problem, where sparsity is promoted in the wavelet domain: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \underset{C_{1},C_{2},...C_{k},\mathbf{w}}{\text{argmax}} \mathbf{w}^T\mathcal{D} \\ & s.t. \quad \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{B}_2(0, 1) \cap \mathcal{B}_1(0, s) \cap \mathbb{R}^T_{+} \\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\mathcal{B}_p(0, r) \in \mathbb{R}^T$ is the $L_p$ ball centered at zero with radius $r$, and $\mathbb{R}^T_{+}$ is the positive orthant, $\mathbb{R}^T_{+} \equiv \{ \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^T, w_j \geq 0, \forall j=1,..,T \}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Sparse K-means in the wavelet domain: maximize $\mathbf{w}^T\mathcal{D}$ over clusters and nonnegative $\mathbf{w}$ in the $L_2$ unit ball and $L_1$ ball of radius $s$.

nodes.name: Sparse K-means objective in the wavelet domain
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & \underset{C_{1},C_{2},...C_{k},\mathbf{w}}{\text{argmax}} \mathbf{w}^T\mathcal{D} \\ & s.t. \quad \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{B}_2(0, 1) \cap \mathcal{B}_1(0, s) \cap \mathbb{R}^T_{+} \\ \end{aligned}
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.label: eq:sparse_k_means_wavelet_ver2

nodes.name: Sparse K-means algorithm
nodes.statement: In \cite{witten2010framework} the authors propose an iterative algorithm for solving Problem (\ref{eq:sparse_k_means_wavelet_ver2}), where each iteration consists of updating the clusters $C_j$ by running K-means, and updating $\mathbf{w}$ with a closed-form expression. The tuning parameter $s$ is set by the permutation-based Gap Statistic method \cite{tibshirani2001estimating}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Alternate K-means updates of the clusters with closed-form updates of the weights $\mathbf{w}$; $s$ chosen by the gap statistic.

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: each iteration consists of updating the clusters $C_j$ by running K-means, and updating $\mathbf{w}$ with a closed-form expression
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Iterate

nodes.name: Update clusters by K-means
nodes.statement: updating the clusters $C_j$ by running K-means
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Update clusters by K-means

nodes.name: Closed-form weight update
nodes.statement: updating $\mathbf{w}$ with a closed-form expression
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form weight update

nodes.name: Choose $s$ by the gap statistic
nodes.statement: The tuning parameter $s$ is set by the permutation-based Gap Statistic method \cite{tibshirani2001estimating}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Sparse Clustering with Wavelets -- Univariate Signals
nodes.statement_short: Choose $s$ by the gap statistic

nodes.name: Partition and group sub-vector
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a partition of $\{1,..,T\}$ and denote by $\mathbf{v}_{(g)}$ the elements of $w$ corresponding to group $g \in \mathcal{G}$.

nodes.name: Group size
nodes.statement: Let $|g|$ the number of elements in $g$.

nodes.name: Group norm
nodes.statement: Define the group-norm with respect to the partition $\mathcal{G}$ \cite{bach2011convex}, \begin{equation} || \mathbf{v} ||_{\mathcal{G}} \equiv \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \sqrt{|g|} || \mathbf{v}_{(g)} ||_2 \end{equation} where we multiply the vector norms $|| \mathbf{v}_{(g)} ||_2$ by $\sqrt{|g|}$ as in \cite{chen2012compressive} and \cite{friedman2010note}, to give greater penalties to larger groups (other coefficients may also be used).
nodes.statement_short: Group norm: sum over groups of $\sqrt{|g|}$ times the $L_2$ norm of the group's sub-vector.

nodes.name: Group norm
nodes.statement: || \mathbf{v} ||_{\mathcal{G}} \equiv \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \sqrt{|g|} || \mathbf{v}_{(g)} ||_2
nodes.label: def:group_norm

nodes.name: Group-sparse K-means problem
nodes.statement: Using the group norm, we define the group-sparse K-means problem, where the tuning-parameter $s$ controls group sparsity, with ${\mathcal{B}_{(\mathcal{G})}}(0, s)$ the ball of radius $s$ centered at zero with respect to the group norm $|| \cdot ||_{\mathcal{G}}$. \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \underset{C_{1},C_{2},...C_{K},\mathbf{w}}{\text{argmax}} \mathbf{w}^T\mathcal{D} \\ & s.t. \quad \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{B}_2(0, 1) \cap {\mathcal{B}_{(\mathcal{G})}}(0, s) \cap \mathbb{R}^T_{+} \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Group-sparse K-means: sparse K-means with the $L_1$ constraint replaced by a group-norm ball of radius $s$.

nodes.name: Group-sparse K-means objective
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & \underset{C_{1},C_{2},...C_{K},\mathbf{w}}{\text{argmax}} \mathbf{w}^T\mathcal{D} \\ & s.t. \quad \mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{B}_2(0, 1) \cap {\mathcal{B}_{(\mathcal{G})}}(0, s) \cap \mathbb{R}^T_{+} \end{aligned}
nodes.label: problem_group_sparse

nodes.name: Group-sparse K-means generalizes sparse K-means
nodes.statement: Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) generalizes the sparse K-means problem in eq. (\ref{eq:sparse_k_means_wavelet_ver2}), which is obtained here by setting all groups to have size $1$.
assumptions: setting all groups to have size $1$
conclusions: Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) generalizes the sparse K-means problem in eq. (\ref{eq:sparse_k_means_wavelet_ver2})

nodes.name: Element-wise square root and product
nodes.statement: ($\sqrt{\cdot}$ and $\odot$ in step (a.) represent element-wise vector operations: $[\sqrt{\mathbf{w}}]_j = \sqrt{w_j}$ and $[\mathbf{w} \odot \mathbf{v}]_j = w_j v_j$).

nodes.name: Weight step as an SOCP
nodes.statement: Optimization $w.r.t$ $\mathbf{w}$ can be done with standard Second Order Cone Programming (SOCP) solvers by introducing auxiliary variables.
nodes.statement_short: The weight update is a second-order cone program, solvable with standard SOCP solvers.

nodes.name: Group-Sparse K-means
nodes.statement: {\bf Input:} $\mathbf{v}^{(1)},\mathbf{v}^{(2)},...,\mathbf{v}^{(n)}$, $K$, $iters$, $\mathcal{G}$, $s$ \\ {\bf Output:} Clusters $C_1,C_2,...,C_K$ \begin{enumerate} \item \textbf{Initialize}: Set $w_1=w_2=...=w_T=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ \item \textbf{for} i=$1:iters$ \begin{enumerate} \item Apply K-means on $\sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(1)},..., \sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(n)}$ \item Hold $C_1,...,C_K$ fixed, solve (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) w.r.t $\mathbf{w}$, with tuning parameter $s$ and partition $\mathcal{G}$ \end{enumerate} \item \textbf{Return} $C_1,...,C_K$ \end{enumerate} \protect\caption{Group-Sparse K-means}
nodes.statement_short: Alternate K-means on $\sqrt{\mathbf{w}}$-weighted features with solving the group-sparse weight problem for fixed clusters.
nodes.label: alg:group_sparse_kmeans

nodes.name: Initialize uniform weights
nodes.statement: \textbf{Initialize}: Set $w_1=w_2=...=w_T=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$

nodes.name: Iterate iters times
nodes.statement: \textbf{for} i=$1:iters$ \begin{enumerate} \item Apply K-means on $\sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(1)},..., \sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(n)}$ \item Hold $C_1,...,C_K$ fixed, solve (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) w.r.t $\mathbf{w}$, with tuning parameter $s$ and partition $\mathcal{G}$

nodes.name: K-means on weighted features
nodes.statement: Apply K-means on $\sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(1)},..., \sqrt{\mathbf{w}} \odot \mathbf{v}^{(n)}$
nodes.statement_short: Run K-means on the $\sqrt{\mathbf{w}}$-scaled coefficient vectors.

nodes.name: Solve for weights
nodes.statement: Hold $C_1,...,C_K$ fixed, solve (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) w.r.t $\mathbf{w}$, with tuning parameter $s$ and partition $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement_short: With clusters fixed, solve the group-sparse problem for $\mathbf{w}$.

nodes.name: Return clusters
nodes.statement: \textbf{Return} $C_1,...,C_K$

nodes.name: Scale-based wavelet group partition
nodes.statement: Therefore, we define the partitions $\mathcal{G} = \big\{ g_j = \{w_{2^j},...,w_{2^{j+1}-1}\} , j=0,..\log_2(T) \big\}$ with $|g_j| = 2^{j}$, and solve Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) with the group norm defined by $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.1 Exploiting Structure of Wavelet Coefficients using Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: Groups are the wavelet scales: $g_j$ holds the $2^j$ coefficients at level $j$.

nodes.name: Other group structures for wavelet trees
nodes.statement: Our choice of $\mathcal{G}$ in this work is not the only one possible exploiting the structure of the wavelets coefficients tree - for example, one may also choose groups corresponding to connected sub-trees (particular nodes and all of their descendent in the tree). Finally, by allowing partitions $\mathcal{G}$ with group overlaps, it is possible to get a richer structure for wavelet coefficients, for example by using tree-structured sparsity as in \cite{chen2012compressive}.
nodes.section: 3.3.1 Exploiting Structure of Wavelet Coefficients using Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: Alternatives: groups as connected sub-trees, or overlapping groups giving tree-structured sparsity.

nodes.name: Multivariate signal instance
nodes.statement: Let each instance $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$ be a multivariate signal, represented as a matrix $\mathbf{X}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{G\times T}$ where $G$ is the number of variables and $T$ as above (See Figure \ref{fig:data_multi}).
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity

nodes.name: Multivariate group-sparse clustering
nodes.statement: We transform each row of $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$ with DWT to get $\mathbf{V}^{(i)}$. We then concatenate the rows of each $\mathbf{V}^{(i)}$ into one vector of length $G\times T$ and solve Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) with the group norm $\mathcal{G}$ defined by $\mathcal{G} = \big\{ g_t = \{ {t},{t+T},\ldots,{t+GT}\}, t = 1,..,T \big\}$. Each group corresponds to a ``vertical time-frequency slice" across the $G$ univariate signals comprising $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: DWT each variable, concatenate, and solve group-sparse K-means with groups = the same time-frequency coordinate across the $G$ variables.

nodes.name: Row-wise DWT
nodes.statement: We transform each row of $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$ with DWT to get $\mathbf{V}^{(i)}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: Row-wise DWT

nodes.name: Concatenate rows
nodes.statement: We then concatenate the rows of each $\mathbf{V}^{(i)}$ into one vector of length $G\times T$
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: Concatenate rows

nodes.name: Solve with slice groups
nodes.statement: solve Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) with the group norm $\mathcal{G}$ defined by $\mathcal{G} = \big\{ g_t = \{ {t},{t+T},\ldots,{t+GT}\}, t = 1,..,T \big\}$.

nodes.name: Groups are vertical time-frequency slices
nodes.statement: Each group corresponds to a ``vertical time-frequency slice" across the $G$ univariate signals comprising $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: Groups are vertical time-frequency slices

nodes.name: Prior behind the multivariate grouping
nodes.statement: Intuitively, this structure reflects the prior assumption that if at some point $t$ on the time-frequency axis we have an ``active clustering feature", then we expect it to be active across all $G$ univariate signals comprising each $\mathbf{X}^{(i)}$, but also enables flexibility by allowing $\{w_{t},w_{t+T},\ldots,w_{t+GT}\}$ to be different.
nodes.section: 3.3.2 Clustering Multivariate Signals with Group Sparsity
nodes.statement_short: An active clustering feature at time-frequency point $t$ is expected active in all $G$ variables, with weights still free to differ.

nodes.name: Wavelet transform is not translation invariant
nodes.statement: The wavelet transform is not invariant to translations and scaling.
conclusions: The wavelet transform is not invariant to translations and scaling.

nodes.name: Instability of fine wavelet coefficients
nodes.statement: In addition, while the coarse-grain coefficients are stable under small deformations, the fine resolution coefficients are unstable \cite{mallat2012group}.
conclusions: the coarse-grain coefficients are stable under small deformations
the fine resolution coefficients are unstable

nodes.name: Scattering transform
nodes.statement: To overcome the effects of the above transformations we use the scattering transform \cite{mallat2012group}, a recent extension of wavelets which is stable to such deformations. The scattering representation of a signal is built with a non-linear, unitary transform computed in a manner resembling a deep convolutional network where filter coefficients are given by a wavelet operator \cite{anden2014deep}.
differentia: which is stable to such deformations
nodes.statement_short: Scattering transform: a deformation-stable, unitary, nonlinear extension of wavelets computed like a convolutional network.

nodes.name: Zeroth scattering layer
nodes.statement: For a function $f(t)$ the $0$-th scattering layer is obtained by a convolution, \begin{equation} S^{(0)} \equiv f \star \phi \end{equation} where $f \star g(t) \equiv \int_{s=-\infty}^{\infty} f(s) g(t-s) ds$ and $\phi$ is an averaging filter.

nodes.name: Zeroth scattering layer
nodes.statement: S^{(0)} \equiv f \star \phi
nodes.label: eq:scat_layer1

nodes.name: First-layer wavelet filter bank
nodes.statement: Let $\{\Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}\}_{j_1 \in J_1}$ be a filter-bank containing different dilations of a complex mother wavelet function $\Psi$ for a set of indices $J_1$, with $\Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}(t) = a_1^{j_1} \Psi(a_1^{j_1} t)$.
differentia: containing different dilations of a complex mother wavelet function $\Psi$

nodes.name: First scattering layer
nodes.statement: To regain translation invariance lost by applying $\Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}$, we perform an additional convolution step with $\phi$ and obtain the scattering functions of the first layer: \begin{equation} S_{j_1}^{(1)} \equiv |f \star \Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}| \star \phi, \quad \forall j_1 \in J_1 \end{equation} where the absolute value $|\cdot|$ is a contraction operator - this operator reduces pairwise distances between signals, and prevents explosion of the energy propagated to deeper scattering layers \cite{mallat2012group}.

nodes.name: First scattering layer
nodes.statement: S_{j_1}^{(1)} \equiv |f \star \Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}| \star \phi, \quad \forall j_1 \in J_1
nodes.label: eq:scat_layer2

nodes.name: Second-layer filters
nodes.statement: To recover the high frequencies lost by averaging, we again take convolutions of $|x \star \Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}|$, with $\Psi^{(2)}_{j_2}$ for some $j_2 \in J_2$.

nodes.name: Layer-l wavelet filters
nodes.statement: More generally, define $\Psi^{(l)}_{j_l}(t) = a_l^{j_l} \Psi(a_l^{j_l} t)$ where $a_l$ determines the dilation frequency resolution at layer $l$.

nodes.name: Scale path
nodes.statement: For a scattering layer $l$, let $(j_1,..,j_l)$ define a \textit{scale path} along the scattering network.

nodes.name: l-th scattering layer
nodes.statement: This process above continues in the same way, with the scattering functions at the $l$-th layer given by \begin{equation} S^{(l)}_{j_1,..,j_{l}} \equiv | .. ||f \star \Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}| \star \Psi^{(2)}_{j_2}| \star \Psi^{(3)}_{j_3}| \star,...,\star \Psi^{(l)}_{j_l}| \star \phi, \: \forall (j_1,..,j_l) \in J_1 \times J_2 \times .. \times J_l. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Layer-$l$ scattering: iterate wavelet convolution and modulus along the scale path, then average with $\phi$.

nodes.name: l-th scattering layer
nodes.statement: S^{(l)}_{j_1,..,j_{l}} \equiv | .. ||f \star \Psi^{(1)}_{j_1}| \star \Psi^{(2)}_{j_2}| \star \Psi^{(3)}_{j_3}| \star,...,\star \Psi^{(l)}_{j_l}| \star \phi, \: \forall (j_1,..,j_l) \in J_1 \times J_2 \times .. \times J_l.
nodes.label: eq:scat_layerk

nodes.name: Scattering coefficients
nodes.statement: The corresponding scattering coefficients $v_{j_1,..,j_l}^{(l)}(t)$ are obtained by evaluating $S_{j_1,..,j_l}^{(l)}$ at time $t$.

nodes.name: Sampling resolution
nodes.statement: In practice, we let a resolution parameter $\Delta_t$ determine the points at which we evaluate $S^{(l)}_{j_1,..,j_{l}}$, where for each $S^{(L)}_{j_1,..,j_l}$ we only sample at points $t = \frac{k\Delta_t}{2}$ with $k = 0,\ldots, \lceil\frac{2T}{\Delta_t}\rceil$.

nodes.name: Final scattering layer
nodes.statement: We stop the process when reaching the final scattering layer $L$, obtaining scattering coefficients in layers $l=0,1,..,L$.

nodes.name: Scattering yields sparse representations
nodes.statement: We empirically found that in many cases the scattering transform can give a sparse representation of signals, and that this sparsity helps in the clustering task (see Section \ref{sec:real_data} for real-data results).
conclusions: the scattering transform can give a sparse representation of signals
this sparsity helps in the clustering task

nodes.name: Scattering group structure
nodes.statement: For each function $S^{(l)}_{j_1,..,j_{l}}$, we group all coefficients resulting from the evaluation of this function. We thus solve Problem (\ref{problem_group_sparse}) with the following definition of groups: \begin{equation} \mathcal{G} = \big\{ g_{j_1,...,j_l}, \forall l=0,..,L, \forall (j_1,...,j_l) \in J_1 \times .. \times J_l \big\} \end{equation} where \begin{equation} g_{j_1,j_2,...,j_l}= \Big\{v_{j_1,\ldots,j_l}^{(l)}(\frac{k\Delta_t}{2}): k = 0,\ldots, \lceil\frac{2T}{\Delta_t}\rceil \Big\} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: One group per scattering function $S^{(l)}_{j_1..j_l}$: all its sampled coefficients.

nodes.name: Scattering group partition
nodes.statement: \mathcal{G} = \big\{ g_{j_1,...,j_l}, \forall l=0,..,L, \forall (j_1,...,j_l) \in J_1 \times .. \times J_l \big\}

nodes.name: Group sparsity helps for few signals (univariate)
nodes.statement: Group sparsity improved accuracy substantially when the number of curves $n$ is particularly low (and thus so is SNR).
assumptions: when the number of curves $n$ is particularly low
conclusions: Group sparsity improved accuracy substantially

nodes.name: Unconstrained sparse K-means catches up for large n
nodes.statement: When $n$ grows, the more flexible method that does not impose group constraints picks up and the two methods reach about the same accuracy.
conclusions: the two methods reach about the same accuracy

nodes.name: Group sparsity helps for multivariate signals
nodes.statement: Group sparsity improved clustering accuracy substantially, especially for low $n$.
conclusions: Group sparsity improved clustering accuracy substantially, especially for low $n$.

nodes.name: Scattering improves accuracy on all real datasets
nodes.statement: In all cases, using the scattering transform improved clustering accuracy.
conclusions: using the scattering transform improved clustering accuracy

nodes.name: Scattering with sparse clustering improves Berkeley growth accuracy
nodes.statement: We applied the scattering transform together with sparse clustering, which lead to substantial improvements in accuracy.
conclusions: We applied the scattering transform together with sparse clustering, which lead to substantial improvements in accuracy.

nodes.name: Sparse K-means equals K-means on Berkeley scattering features
nodes.statement: Applying sparse K-means on the scattering features led to the about the same results as ordinary K-means in this feature space, with $ARI=0.87$).
conclusions: led to the about the same results as ordinary K-means in this feature space

nodes.name: SPARCWave feature selection then K-means
nodes.statement: The features with high-magnitude coefficients can, however, be used in standard K-means, viewing SPARCWave\: as a feature-selection step \cite{witten2010framework}. We can select all non-zero features $w_j$ (or above some threshold) and apply K-means using only these features.
nodes.statement_short: Use SPARCWave as feature selection: keep features with non-zero (or large) weights $w_j$ and rerun K-means on them.

nodes.name: Keep non-zero-weight features
nodes.statement: We can select all non-zero features $w_j$ (or above some threshold)
nodes.statement_short: Keep non-zero-weight features

nodes.name: K-means on selected features
nodes.statement: apply K-means using only these features
nodes.statement_short: K-means on selected features

nodes.name: Feature selection raises Berkeley ARI
nodes.statement: This technique improved accuracy from $0.87$ to $0.91$.
conclusions: This technique improved accuracy from $0.87$ to $0.91$.

nodes.name: Group sparsity neutral on Berkeley
nodes.statement: Group-sparse clustering with the scattering transform lead to similar results, possibly due to the very short signal length $T$ (see Table \ref{tab:results_real_data} and Figure \ref{fig:real}).
conclusions: Group-sparse clustering with the scattering transform lead to similar results

nodes.name: Log-frequency scattering gives frequency-scaling invariance
nodes.statement: By applying the scattering transform on data in the log-frequency domain, we obtain invariance to translation in log-frequency and consequently to scaling in frequency.
assumptions: applying the scattering transform on data in the log-frequency domain
conclusions: we obtain invariance to translation in log-frequency and consequently to scaling in frequency

nodes.name: Group sparsity neutral on Phoneme
nodes.statement: Here too group-sparse clustering did not change accuracy, possibly due to large sample size (see Table \ref{tab:results_real_data} and Figure \ref{fig:phoneme_real} in the Appendix).
conclusions: group-sparse clustering did not change accuracy

nodes.name: Scattering with sparse clustering improves Wheat accuracy
nodes.statement: Applying the scattering transform in combination with sparse clustering improved accuracy significantly.
conclusions: Applying the scattering transform in combination with sparse clustering improved accuracy significantly.

nodes.name: Group sparsity hurts on Wheat
nodes.statement: However, using group sparsity reduced accuracy, perhaps because out of $924$ features only $2$ are found to have non-zero weights (see Table \ref{tab:results_real_data} and Figure \ref{fig:wheat_real} in the Appendix).
conclusions: using group sparsity reduced accuracy

nodes.name: SPARCScatter is best on all datasets
nodes.statement: The SPARCScatter\: method shows superior clustering accuracy over all datasets.
conclusions: The SPARCScatter\: method shows superior clustering accuracy over all datasets.

nodes.name: Theoretical guarantees for (group) sparse clustering
nodes.statement: Finally, there are few known theoretical guarantees for sparse-clustering methods, and it would be interesting to develop such guarantees to the framework in \cite{witten2010framework} and it's group extension we have proposed.
nodes.statement_short: Develop theoretical guarantees for sparse K-means and its group-sparse extension.

nodes.name: Adjusted Rand Index
nodes.statement: To evaluate the clustering performance we used the {\it Adjusted Rand Index} ($ARI$) as a measure of clustering accuracy \cite{wagner2007comparing}, defined as: \begin{equation} ARI \equiv \frac{\sum_{i < j} \binom{n_{ij}}{2} - \frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}} [\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2}] [\sum_j \binom{b_j}{2}] } { \frac{1}{2} [\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2} + \sum_{j} \binom{b_j}{2}] - \frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}} [\sum_i \binom{a_i}{2}] [\sum_j \binom{b_j}{2}] } \end{equation} where $a_i$ denotes the number of signals whose true cluster is $i$, , $b_j$ the number of signals assigned to cluster $j$ and $n_{ij}$ the number of signals whose true cluster is $i$ and are assigned to cluster $j$, with $n=\sum_i a_i = \sum_j b_j = \sum_{i,j} n_{ij}$.
nodes.statement_short: ARI: chance-corrected agreement between true and assigned clusters, from the contingency counts $n_{ij}$, $a_i$, $b_j$.

nodes.name: Adjusted Rand Index

nodes.label: def:adjusted_rand_index
